This document is reference material for the deterministic functions that are used in this
book and for several others that are common in ecology. For each function it gives the
formula, its properties, R code and a description of when the function is useful.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) explains the tools with which the properties are
derived (limits, derivatives and special points), so the entries apply these tools without
explaining them again.

Every entry has the same parts: a summary of the function, a description of when it is
useful and of where it comes from, and its formula with the derivation of its landmarks.

The symbols are those of Chapter 5. The input is $x$ and the output is $y=f(x)$. The
parameters are called $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$: these letters are positions in a formula, and
every entry says what each of them controls and which units it has. Unless an entry says
otherwise, the parameters are positive and $x\ge0$. The R functions use the same letters
as the formulas, including `c` (R keeps functions and other objects apart, so `c()` still
combines values). The papers cited in the entries are listed in @sec-fn-references.

The content of this document has been derived from Chapter 3 of *Ecological Models and Data in R*
by Benjamin Bolker (2008). The description of how these models are often applied and examples
of scientific articles where that happens are also taken from this chapter.

# Choosing a function {#sec-fn-overview}

The table below lists the functions of this supplement by the properties that we can see
in a plot of data: the values of $x$ for which the function is used, how it starts, how it
ends and what happens in between.
[Choosing a function](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-choosing-function) in Chapter 5 explains
how to use these properties to select candidates for a response, and
[Starting values by eye](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-starting-values) how to read values
of the parameters from a plot.

| Function | Formula | Domain | Left end | Right end | Middle |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [Linear](#sec-fn-linear) | $a+bx$ | all $x$ | straight line | straight line | monotonic |
| [Quadratic](#sec-fn-quadratic) | $a+bx+cx^2$ | all $x$ | grows without bound | grows without bound | one maximum or minimum |
| [Threshold](#sec-fn-threshold) | $a$ if $x<c$, $b$ otherwise | all $x$ | flat | flat | one jump |
| [Hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) | $ax$ if $x<c$, $ac$ otherwise | all $x$ | straight line | flat | one breakpoint |
| [Piecewise linear](#sec-fn-piecewise-linear) | two lines joined at $c$ | all $x$ | straight line | straight line | one breakpoint |
| [Hyperbolic](#sec-fn-hyperbolic) | $\dfrac{a}{b+x}$ | $x\ge0$ | finite value | tends to 0 | decreasing |
| [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Holling type III](#sec-fn-holling3) | $\dfrac{ax^2}{b^2+x^2}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid |
| [Holling type IV](#sec-fn-holling4) | $\dfrac{ax^2}{b+cx+x^2}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, accelerating | asymptote | hump before the asymptote when $c<0$ |
| [Exponential](#sec-fn-exponential) | $ae^{-bx}$ | $x\ge0$ | finite value | tends to 0 | decreasing |
| [Saturating exponential](#sec-fn-monomolecular) | $a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right)$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) | $axe^{-bx}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | tends to 0 | one maximum |
| [Logistic](#sec-fn-logistic) | $\dfrac{a}{1+e^{-b(x-c)}}$ | all $x$ | close to 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid |
| [Gompertz](#sec-fn-gompertz) | $a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | all $x$ | close to 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid, asymmetric |
| [Bell-shaped](#sec-fn-gaussian) | $a\,e^{-(x-c)^2/(2b^2)}$ | all $x$ | tends to 0 | tends to 0 | one maximum, symmetric |
| [Power law](#sec-fn-power) | $ax^b$ | $x>0$ | 0 or unbounded | 0 or unbounded | monotonic |
| [von Bertalanffy](#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy) | $a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | $x\ge c$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Shepherd](#sec-fn-shepherd) | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x^c}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote if $c=1$, tends to 0 if $c>1$ | saturating, or one maximum if $c>1$ |
| [Hassell](#sec-fn-hassell) | $\dfrac{ax}{(b+x)^c}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote if $c=1$, tends to 0 if $c>1$ | saturating, or one maximum if $c>1$ |
| [Generalised Ricker](#sec-fn-generalised-ricker) | $a\left[\dfrac{x}{b}\,e^{1-x/b}\right]^c$ | $x\ge0$ | 0 | tends to 0 | one maximum of adjustable width |
| [Non-rectangular hyperbola](#sec-fn-nonrectangular) | $\dfrac{\alpha x+p_{\max}-\sqrt{(\alpha x+p_{\max})^2-4\theta\alpha x\,p_{\max}}}{2\theta}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating, with a bend of adjustable sharpness |
| [Richards](#sec-fn-richards) | $\dfrac{a}{\left[1+d\,e^{-b(x-c)}\right]^{1/d}}$ | all $x$ | close to 0 | asymptote | sigmoid of adjustable asymmetry |

Several functions have the same properties in this table (e.g., the Michaelis–Menten and
the saturating exponential functions). The entries say how such functions differ and
which mechanism, if any, leads to each of them.

# Polynomials

A polynomial is a sum of powers of $x$, each multiplied by a parameter. The two
polynomials that are used most are the straight line and the parabola.

## Linear {#sec-fn-linear}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a + b * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{straight line} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \quad (b \neq 0) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } b \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{crosses zero at } x = -a/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + b(x - c),\ \text{with } d = a + bc \text{ the value at } x = c
\end{aligned}
$$

The linear function describes a response that changes by the same amount for every unit of
the predictor. It is a mechanistic function when a quantity accumulates or is lost at a
constant rate, as the quantity is then a linear function of time. More often it is a
phenomenological description over a limited range of $x$, since any smooth function is
close to a straight line over a short enough interval. In this book
the linear function is mostly used inside another function: $e^{a+bx}$ for a positive
response and $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a+bx)$ for a probability (see
[Range and composition](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition)).

The function is

$$
f(x)=a+bx,
$$

where $a$ is the value of the function at $x=0$ (the intercept) and $b$ is its slope. Both
parameters can be positive or negative. The
[derivative](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-derivatives) is the same at every $x$,

$$
f'(x)=b, \qquad f''(x)=0,
$$

so the function has neither curvature nor special points. It has no asymptote either: as
$x\to\infty$ it grows without bound when $b>0$ and decreases without bound when $b<0$. It
crosses zero at $x=-a/b$, so for a quantity that must be positive the function can only be
used on one side of that value.

The intercept $a$ depends on where the zero of $x$ lies, and it has no meaning when
$x=0$ is far from the values of interest (e.g., when $x$ is a calendar year). In that case
we write the function around a reference value $c$ that we choose,

$$
f(x)=d+b(x-c), \qquad d=a+bc,
$$

where $d$ is the value of the function at $x=c$. This is a
[reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation): the line is the
same, and the slope $b$ keeps its value and its meaning.

## Quadratic {#sec-fn-quadratic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a + b * x + c * x^2| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal when } c < 0;\ \text{U-shaped when } c > 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c < 0;\quad y \geq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope at } x = 0;\quad c = \text{half of the second derivative} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{decreases without bound when } c < 0,\ \text{grows without bound when } c > 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum or minimum at } x_{\max} = -b/(2c),\ \text{with value } a - b^2/(4c) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad f(x_{\max}) + c\,(x - x_{\max})^2
\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic function, or parabola, is the simplest function with a maximum or a minimum.
It is used as a phenomenological description of a response that is highest (or lowest) at
intermediate values of the predictor, over a limited range of $x$. Two examples show how
it is used. In community ecology a quadratic term is added to a straight line to describe
the abundance of a species that has an optimum along an environmental gradient. A parabola
becomes negative far from its maximum and an abundance cannot, so it is usually the
logarithm of the abundance that is taken as a quadratic function, which gives the
[bell-shaped](#sec-fn-gaussian) function (ter Braak and Prentice 1988). In the study of
natural selection the fitness of individuals is described by a quadratic function of a
trait, and the curvature $c$ measures stabilising selection when it is negative (fitness
is highest at an intermediate value of the trait) and disruptive selection when it is
positive (Lande and Arnold 1983). The function can also follow from geometry: a process
that depends on a surface, such as the area of the skin or of the mouth, is quadratic in
the length of the organism. Finally, every smooth function is close to a parabola near
its maximum, which is the idea behind the Wald interval of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty).

Polynomials of a higher order (a cubic function has a term in $x^3$, and so on) add one
bend for every additional power and can follow almost any set of points. However, outside
the range of the data they grow or decrease without bound, in a direction that is decided
by the highest power alone, so their predictions there are unreliable.^[The extrapolation
of census counts with a polynomial is a well-known exercise on this problem; see Forsythe,
Malcolm and Moler (1977).] For that reason this supplement stops at the quadratic
function.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a+bx+cx^2,
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, $b$ is the slope at $x=0$ (in units of $y$ per unit of
$x$) and $c$ controls the curvature (in units of $y$ per unit of $x$ squared). The three
parameters can be positive or negative. The first two derivatives are

$$
f'(x)=b+2cx, \qquad f''(x)=2c.
$$

The second derivative has the same sign everywhere. When $c<0$ the function is concave for
every $x$ and its only [critical point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-maxima) is a
maximum; when $c>0$ it is convex and the critical point is a minimum. Setting $f'(x)=0$:

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{b}{2c}, \qquad f(x_{\max})=a-\frac{b^2}{4c}.
$$

If we complete the square, we can write the function with these two landmarks as
parameters,

$$
f(x)=f(x_{\max})+c\,(x-x_{\max})^2,
$$

which shows that the parabola is symmetric around $x_{\max}$. It also shows that, when
$c<0$, the function crosses zero at $x_{\max}\pm\sqrt{f(x_{\max})/(-c)}$ and is negative
beyond those two values. A response that cannot be negative is therefore described by a
quadratic function only between them.

# Piecewise functions

A piecewise function is defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain.
The parts meet at a **breakpoint**, at which the function, its slope or both change
abruptly. In R these functions are written with `ifelse()` (see
[Functions in R](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-functions-r)).

## Threshold {#sec-fn-threshold}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a, b)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{step} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y = a \text{ or } y = b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value below the threshold (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value from the threshold onwards (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{threshold (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At the left end}: &\quad f(x) = a,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = b,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{jump of size } b - a \text{ at } x = c \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the limit of } a + \dfrac{b - a}{1 + e^{-s(x - c)}} \text{ as } s \to \infty,\ \text{for } x \neq c
\end{aligned}
$$

The threshold function describes a response that switches between two levels when the
predictor crosses a critical value. Two examples show how it is used. Models of optimal
life histories often find that the best strategy is a switch at a critical size.
Monocarpic perennials, which flower once and then die, are a standard case, because a
plant should flower only when it is large enough (Kachi and Hirose 1985), and in the
integral projection models of Rees and Rose (2002) and Childs et al. (2003) the optimal
probability of flowering is a step function of plant size. The flowering of plants in the
field changes more gradually with size than the step that the models predict, so the
function describes the strategy that theory favours and not the shape of the data. The
function is also used as a statistical model of a change-point: a value of an
environmental variable, such as the concentration of a nutrient, at which the mean
response of a community changes from one level to another (Qian et al. 2003). The
function is mechanistic when theory predicts the switch, as in the first example, and
phenomenological when it only describes a change in the data, as in the second.
[Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) uses a threshold function to show what a jump does to
a likelihood.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a & \text{if } x<c \\
b & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the two levels, which can take any value, and $c$ is the threshold.
The formula has to say to which side the value $x=c$ belongs; here it belongs to the upper
piece. There is nothing to derive with calculus. The two limits are the two levels, and
the slope is zero everywhere except at $x=c$, where the function jumps by $b-a$ and has no
derivative. This has a consequence for estimation: moving $c$ by a small amount changes
the function only if an observation lies between the old and the new threshold, so the
methods that search for an optimum by following a slope fail for $c$ (Chapter 8).

A smooth function that approaches the threshold function is the
[logistic](#sec-fn-logistic) function with a lower level $a$,

$$
f(x)=a+\frac{b-a}{1+e^{-s(x-c)}},
$$

where $s$ is the steepness. The larger $s$ is, the shorter the range of $x$ over which the
function moves from $a$ to $b$, and as $s\to\infty$ it becomes the threshold function
everywhere except at the breakpoint: at $x=c$ the logistic function equals $(a+b)/2$ for
every $s$, whereas the threshold function equals $b$.

## Hockey stick {#sec-fn-hockey-stick}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a * x, a * c)} \quad \text{or} \quad \texttt{pmin(a * x, a * c)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a sharp corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ in most uses}) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq ac \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = ac,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{where the slope changes from } a \text{ to } 0 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \min(ax, d),\ \text{with } d = ac \text{ the plateau}
\end{aligned}
$$

The hockey stick function describes a response that increases in proportion to the
predictor until it hits a ceiling. It has a mechanistic reading when a process runs at a
constant rate per unit of $x$ until a capacity is reached, as for filter feeders that
take up food in proportion to its concentration until they reach a maximum uptake (the
Holling type I functional response). It is also used for the number of recruits as a
function of the size of the spawning stock in fisheries (Barrowman and Myers 2000), for
the density dependence of populations of lemmings, sheep and moose (Framstad et al. 1997;
Grenfell et al. 1998; Post et al. 2002) and to locate the edges between habitats in a
landscape (Toms and Lesperance 2003). In models of population dynamics it is also called
a ramp function (Brännström and Sumpter 2005). Bacon and Watts (1971, 1974) studied how
to estimate the transition between two straight lines from data.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
ax & \text{if } x<c \\
ac & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ is the slope of the first piece and $c$ is the breakpoint. The two pieces meet
at $x=c$, where both give $ac$, so the function has no jump. Its slope does: the
derivative is $a$ for $x<c$ and 0 for $x>c$, and it does not exist at the breakpoint. The
plateau $ac$ can be used as a parameter in the place of the breakpoint, which gives
$\min(ax,d)$ with $d=ac$: the smaller of the straight line and the plateau, `pmin()` in R.

It is instructive to compare the hockey stick with the
[Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function that has the same initial slope $a$
and the same upper limit $ac$, which is $acx/(c+x)$. At $x=c$ the hockey stick has reached
its plateau, whereas the Michaelis–Menten function is at half of it: the breakpoint of
the one is the half-maximum of the other. The two functions are the extremes of a family
with a bend of adjustable sharpness, the
[non-rectangular hyperbola](#sec-fn-nonrectangular).

## Piecewise linear {#sec-fn-piecewise-linear}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a + b * x, a + b * c + d * (x - c))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{two straight lines that meet at a corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \text{ when } b \text{ and } d \text{ have the same sign};\quad
y \leq a + bc \text{ when } b > 0 > d \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)};\quad
d = \text{slope above the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \quad (c > 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } d \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a + bc,\ \text{where the slope changes from } b \text{ to } d \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a + bx + (d - b)\max(0,\, x - c)
\end{aligned}
$$

The piecewise linear function describes a response that changes at one constant rate up to
a breakpoint and at another constant rate beyond it. It is the general form of the
functions of this group that have no jump: the [hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) is the
case in which the first line starts at zero and the second one is flat. The function is
used when an organism is expected to switch from one regime to another at some value of
the predictor, for example from growing to reproducing once it has reached a certain size
or age, and to locate ecological thresholds in data (Toms and Lesperance 2003). It is
mechanistic when theory predicts the switch, and otherwise a phenomenological description
of a relationship that bends once.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a+bx & \text{if } x<c \\
a+bc+d\,(x-c) & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, $b$ is the slope below the breakpoint $c$ and $d$ is the
slope above it. The parameters $a$, $b$ and $d$ can be positive or negative. The second
piece starts at $a+bc$, which is the value that the first piece reaches at $x=c$, so the
two lines meet and the function has no jump. Its derivative is $b$ for $x<c$ and $d$ for
$x>c$, and it does not exist at the breakpoint. When $b$ and $d$ have opposite signs the
breakpoint is the maximum ($b>0>d$) or the minimum ($b<0<d$) of the function, and it is
one that we cannot find by setting a derivative to zero.

The function can be written on a single line. The second piece is the first line plus a
correction of the slope that applies only beyond the breakpoint,

$$
f(x)=a+bx+(d-b)\max(0,\,x-c),
$$

where $\max(0,x-c)$ is zero up to the breakpoint and equal to the distance from it
afterwards (`pmax(0, x - c)` in R). In this form $d-b$ is the change in slope at the
breakpoint, and a function with several breakpoints is obtained by adding one such term
for each of them.

A piecewise linear function with many breakpoints can follow any relationship, at the cost
of a corner at each breakpoint. **Splines** remove the corners: they are piecewise cubic
functions whose pieces join smoothly at points called knots. They are used when we want a
smooth curve through the data and do not need to interpret its parameters (Wood 2001,
2006), so they are not described further in this supplement.

# Rational functions

A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials. Its limit as $x\to\infty$ is found by
dividing the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ (see
[Limits and asymptotes](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-limits)). Rational functions
approach their limits slowly, in proportion to a power of $x$.

## Hyperbolic {#sec-fn-hyperbolic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a/b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{numerator (units of } y \text{ times units of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the function has halved (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/b,\ \text{slope } -a/b^2 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the initial value at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{y_0}{1 + x/b},\ \text{with } y_0 = a/b \text{ the value at } x = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The hyperbolic function describes a response that declines towards zero, fast at first and
then more and more slowly. It is used for the performance of an individual as a function
of the density of its neighbours, for example the number of seeds that a plant produces as
a function of the number of plants around it (Pacala and Silander 1987, 1990). The
constant $b$ in the denominator keeps the function finite at $x=0$, where the simpler form
$a/x$ would be infinite. A mechanistic derivation exists when a total saturates: if the
total seed production of a stand follows the Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ of its
density $x$, the production per plant is that total divided by $x$, which is $a/(b+x)$.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{b+x},
$$

where $b$ has the units of $x$ and $a$ has the units of $y$ multiplied by those of $x$.
At $x=0$ the function equals $a/b$, and as $x\to\infty$ the denominator grows without
bound, so $f(x)\to0$. For large $x$ the function is close to $a/x$. Writing it as
$a(b+x)^{-1}$, the power rule and the chain rule give

$$
f'(x)=-\frac{a}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=\frac{2a}{(b+x)^3}.
$$

The slope is negative and the second derivative positive for every $x\ge0$, so the
function decreases and is convex everywhere. Its steepest slope is the one at zero,
$-a/b^2$. The parameter $b$ is a scale parameter (see
[Half-maxima and characteristic scales](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-scales)): if
we solve $a/(b+x)=a/(2b)$ for $x$ we find $x=b$, so $b$ is the value of $x$ at which the
function has fallen to half of its initial value. In the same way it has fallen to a third
at $x=2b$ and to a quarter at $x=3b$. Since the value at zero is easier to read from a
plot than $a$, the function is also written as $y_0/(1+x/b)$ with $y_0=a/b$.

## Michaelis–Menten {#sec-fn-michaelis-menten}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x}{1 + \alpha Hx},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/(\alpha H)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Michaelis–Menten function describes a response that increases in proportion to the
predictor when the predictor is scarce and levels off when it is abundant, because
something else then limits the response. It is one of the two functions of
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd), where its properties are derived step by step, and
it has a different name in almost every field that uses it. In biochemistry it is the rate
of a reaction catalysed by an enzyme as a function of the concentration of the substrate
(Michaelis and Menten 1913), with the parameters written as $v_{\max}$ and $K_m$. In
microbiology it is the Monod equation for the growth rate of micro-organisms on a limiting
nutrient (Monod 1949). In fisheries it is the Beverton–Holt curve for the number of
recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Beverton and Holt 1957). In
ecology it is best known as the Holling type II functional response, the feeding rate of a
predator as a function of the density of its prey (Holling 1959).

The function has a mechanistic derivation in three of these uses.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-mechanistic) derives it for a predator that
divides its time between searching for prey and handling them, and the same argument
applies to an enzyme, which spends a larger fraction of its time bound to the substrate as
the substrate becomes more concentrated. The Beverton–Holt curve follows from a mortality
rate of the young fish that increases linearly with their density (Quinn and Deriso 1999).
The Monod equation is the exception: it has the same form, but it is an empirical
description of the growth rates that are measured in cultures. In that use the function is
phenomenological, as it is whenever it is chosen only because the response rises from zero
and saturates.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, with the units of $y$, and $b$ is the half-maximum, with the
units of $x$. Chapter 5 shows that $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)\to a$ as $x\to\infty$, and that

$$
f'(x)=\frac{ab}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=-\frac{2ab}{(b+x)^3},
$$

so the function increases and is concave for every $x\ge0$, with an initial slope of
$a/b$. To find the value of $x$ at which the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its
asymptote we solve $f(x_p)=pa$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a\,x_p}{b+x_p} &= pa \\
x_p &= p\,(b+x_p) \\
x_p &= \frac{p}{1-p}\,b .
\end{aligned}
$$

For $p=1/2$ this gives the half-maximum, $x_{1/2}=b$. For $p=0.9$ it gives $9b$ and for
$p=0.95$ it gives $19b$: the function approaches its asymptote slowly, and data that stop
at a few times the half-maximum are still far below it.

The parameterisations in use differ in which two landmarks they take as parameters (see
[Reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)):

| Parameters | Formula | Conversion |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Asymptote $a$ and half-maximum $b$ | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x}$ | |
| Attack rate $\alpha$ and handling time $H$ (Holling type II) | $\dfrac{\alpha x}{1+\alpha Hx}$ | $a=1/H$, $b=1/(\alpha H)$ |
| Asymptote $a$ and initial slope $s$ | $\dfrac{asx}{a+sx}$ | $s=a/b$ |

The attack rate $\alpha$ of the second form is the initial slope $s$ of the third one.

## Holling type III {#sec-fn-holling3}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b;\ \text{inflection point at } x = b/\sqrt{3},\ \text{with value } a/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x^2}{1 + \alpha Hx^2},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/\sqrt{\alpha H}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Holling type III function describes a response that increases slowly when the
predictor is scarce, accelerates and then levels off. It is the
[Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function with $x$ replaced by $x^2$ and the
half-maximum by its square, which turns a saturating function into a sigmoid one. As a
functional response it describes predators that kill a smaller proportion of the prey when
the prey are rare, which can result from predators that switch from rare to common prey,
from predators that aggregate where prey are abundant and from other forms of
heterogeneity (Morris 1997). A mechanistic derivation exists: if the attack rate of the
[disc equation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-mechanistic) is proportional to the density
of the prey, $\alpha x$ in the place of $\alpha$, the equation becomes
$\alpha x^2/(1+\alpha Hx^2)$. Hassell et al. (1977) obtained sigmoid functional responses
in this way, from an attack rate that increases with the density of the prey.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b^2+x^2},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, with the units of $y$, and $b$ is the half-maximum, with the
units of $x$. At $x=0$ the function is zero. For small $x$ the denominator is close to
$b^2$, so $f(x)\approx(a/b^2)\,x^2$: the function starts as a parabola, with a slope of
zero. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $x^2$ gives $a/(b^2/x^2+1)$, which
tends to $a$ as $x\to\infty$. The quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b^2+x^2\right)-ax^2\times2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}
=\frac{2ab^2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{2ab^2\left(b^2-3x^2\right)}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The slope is positive for every $x>0$, so the function increases. The second derivative is
zero where $b^2-3x^2=0$, positive below that value and negative above it, so the
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) is at

$$
x=\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\approx0.58\,b, \qquad
f\left(\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{a\,b^2/3}{b^2+b^2/3}=\frac{a}{4},
$$

where the slope has its largest value, $3\sqrt{3}\,a/(8b)\approx0.65\,a/b$. Unlike the
logistic function, the Holling type III function is asymmetric: it is steepest at a
quarter of its asymptote.

To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve
$x_p^2=p\left(b^2+x_p^2\right)$, which gives

$$
x_p=b\sqrt{\frac{p}{1-p}}.
$$

For $p=1/2$ this is the half-maximum, $x_{1/2}=b$, and for $p=0.9$ it is $3b$, against
$9b$ for the Michaelis–Menten function: the square makes the function approach its
asymptote faster. In the form with the attack rate, $H$ is the handling time and $\alpha$
has the units of $y$ per unit of $x$ squared, with $a=1/H$ and $b=1/\sqrt{\alpha H}$.

## Holling type IV {#sec-fn-holling4}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid when } c \geq 0;\ \text{unimodal, with an asymptote, when } c < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y \leq 4ab/(4b - c^2) \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b > 0 \text{ (units of } x \text{ squared)};\quad c \text{ (units of } x\text{), with } c^2 < 4b \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{from below when } c \geq 0 \text{ and from above when } c < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c < 0,\ \text{maximum at } x = -2b/c \text{ with value } 4ab/(4b - c^2) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{with } c = 0,\ \text{the Holling type III function } ax^2/(b + x^2)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Holling type IV function adds a term in $x$ to the denominator of the
[Holling type III](#sec-fn-holling3) function, and the sign of its parameter $c$ decides
the shape. When $c>0$ the function is sigmoid, and it has a mechanistic derivation: it is
the functional response of a predator whose attack rate is itself a Michaelis–Menten
function of the density of the prey, that is, a predator that pursues prey more actively
when they are abundant (Turchin 2003). When $c<0$ the function rises above its asymptote,
reaches a maximum and declines towards the asymptote. In that form it is used
phenomenologically for the intake of a consumer that declines at high density, as a
result of interference among predators or of defences induced in the prey (Holt 1983;
Collings 1997; Wilmshurst et al. 1999; Chen 2004).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b+cx+x^2},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, $b$ is positive and has the units of $x$ squared, and $c$ has
the units of $x$ and can be positive or negative. Note that $b$ is here the counterpart
of $b^2$ in the Holling type III function. The limits are found as for that function:
$f(0)=0$ with a slope of zero, since $f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x^2$ for small $x$, and
$f(x)\to a$ as $x\to\infty$, since dividing by $x^2$ gives $a/(b/x^2+c/x+1)$. The
denominator has to stay positive for every $x\ge0$. That is always so when $c\ge0$. When
$c<0$ the denominator is smallest at $x=-c/2$, where it equals $b-c^2/4$, so the function
requires $c^2<4b$.

The quotient rule gives a derivative whose numerator simplifies:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b+cx+x^2\right)-ax^2\left(c+2x\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2} \\
&= \frac{ax\left(2b+cx\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

A quotient is zero only where its numerator is zero (see
[Maxima and minima](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-maxima)), so the critical points
are $x=0$ and the solution of $2b+cx=0$. When $c\ge0$ the factor $2b+cx$ is positive for
every $x\ge0$ and the function increases throughout. When $c<0$ the slope is positive up
to

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{2b}{c}
$$

and negative beyond it, so this is a maximum. Its value follows from substituting
$x_{\max}$ in the function. The denominator is $b-2b+4b^2/c^2=b\left(4b-c^2\right)/c^2$
and the numerator is $4ab^2/c^2$, so

$$
f(x_{\max})=\frac{4ab}{4b-c^2},
$$

which is larger than $a$: the function overshoots its asymptote and returns to it from
above. The closer $c^2$ is to $4b$, the higher the peak.

# Exponential functions

The functions of this group are built from the exponential function $e^{-bx}$, in which
the parameter $b$ is a rate with the inverse units of $x$. They approach their limits
faster than the rational functions of the same shape, because an exponential dominates any
power of $x$.

## Exponential {#sec-fn-exponential}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex (decay)};\quad \text{increasing, convex (growth, } ae^{bx}\text{)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } -ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{halves every } \log 2/b;\ \text{falls by a factor } e \text{ every } 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad e^{d - bx} \text{ with } d = \log a
\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function describes a quantity that changes by a constant proportion for
every unit of the predictor. It is mechanistic whenever the rate of change of a quantity
is proportional to the quantity itself: a cohort in which every individual has the same
risk of dying per unit of time, litter that loses a constant fraction of its mass per year
as it decomposes (Olson 1963), or light that loses a constant fraction of its intensity in
every layer of leaves of a canopy (Monsi and Saeki 1953). With a positive exponent, $ae^{bx}$, it describes the
growth of a population in which every individual reproduces at a constant rate.

The function is

$$
f(x)=ae^{-bx},
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, since $e^{0}=1$, and $b$ is the rate of decline. As
$x\to\infty$, $e^{-bx}=1/e^{bx}\to0$, so $f(x)\to0$. The rule for a constant multiple and
the rule for the exponential give $f'(x)=-ab\,e^{-bx}=-b\,f(x)$: the slope is negative for
every $x$, and at any point it is proportional to the value of the function. The second derivative,
$f''(x)=ab^2e^{-bx}$, is positive, so the function is convex.

The function has no special point, and what characterises it is a scale. An increase of
$x$ by one unit multiplies the function by $e^{-b}$, wherever we start, so a fraction
$1-e^{-b}$ is lost per unit of $x$. To find the distance over which the function falls to
a fraction $p$ of its value we solve $e^{-bx}=p$:

$$
x_p=\frac{\log(1/p)}{b}.
$$

For $p=1/2$ this is the half-life $\log 2/b\approx0.69/b$, for $p=1/e$ it is the
characteristic scale $1/b$, and for $p=0.05$ it is $\log(20)/b\approx3/b$. For exponential
growth the same algebra gives the doubling time, $\log 2/b$.

Taking logarithms gives $\log f(x)=\log a-bx$: on a plot with a logarithmic $y$ axis the
exponential function is a straight line with slope $-b$. In the other direction, the exponential of a straight line, $e^{d-bx}$, is an exponential
function with $a=e^{d}$. This is the form used when the function is the mean of a count,
since it is positive for any value of $d$ and $b$.

## Saturating exponential {#sec-fn-monomolecular}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * x))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = \log 2/b;\ \text{a fraction } 1 - 1/e \text{ of the asymptote at } x = 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + a\left(1 - e^{-bx}\right),\ \text{which starts at } d \text{ and approaches } d + a
\end{aligned}
$$

The saturating exponential function describes a response that approaches an upper limit,
at a rate that is proportional to the distance that remains to that limit. This is its
mechanism, and it appears under several names. It is also called the
monomolecular function. In epidemiology it is the catalytic curve, the fraction of a cohort that has
been infected by a given age when the risk of infection per unit of time is constant
(Anderson and May 1991). It is the simplest form of the
[von Bertalanffy](#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy) growth curve (Essington et al. 2001), and it
was used by Skellam (1951) for the number of offspring as a function of the number of
adults (see also Brännström and Sumpter 2005). In this book it is the response function
of the practical of [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) and of
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd).

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote and $b$ is the rate at which the function approaches it. At
$x=0$ the exponential equals 1 and $f(0)=0$; as $x\to\infty$ the exponential tends to
zero and $f(x)\to a$. The derivatives are

$$
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab^2e^{-bx},
$$

so the function increases, with an initial slope $ab$, and is concave everywhere. Note
that $f'(x)=b\left(a-f(x)\right)$: the slope is proportional to the distance to the
asymptote. To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve
$1-e^{-bx}=p$:

$$
x_p=\frac{\log\left(1/(1-p)\right)}{b}.
$$

The half-maximum is $x_{1/2}=\log 2/b$. At the characteristic scale $x=1/b$ the function
has reached $1-1/e\approx63\%$ of its asymptote, and it reaches 90% at
$\log(10)/b\approx2.3/b$. A [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function with the
same asymptote and the same initial slope has its half-maximum at $1/b$ and reaches 90%
only at $9/b$, so the saturating exponential bends more sharply towards its asymptote.

Two shifted and scaled forms of this function are used in later chapters (see
[Shifting and scaling](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts)). The first one adds
a value at zero,

$$
f(x)=d+a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
$$

which starts at $d$ and approaches $d+a$; Chapters 6 and 7 write it as
$r+a\left(1-e^{-kx}\right)$ for the response of photosynthesis to light. The second one
takes the value at zero, $y_0$, and the asymptote, $y_\infty$, as parameters,

$$
f(x)=y_\infty-\left(y_\infty-y_0\right)e^{-bx},
$$

and it is the same function with $d=y_0$ and $a=y_\infty-y_0$; the practical of Chapter 7
writes it as $A-(A-R_0)e^{-kt}$ for the growth of trees.

## Ricker {#sec-fn-ricker}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a/(be) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = 1/b \text{ with value } a/(be);\ \text{inflection point at } x = 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,x\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad x\,e^{r(1 - x/K)} \text{ with } a = e^{r},\ b = r/K
\end{aligned}
$$

The Ricker function describes a response that increases in proportion to the predictor
when the predictor is small, reaches a maximum and declines towards zero. Ricker (1954)
proposed it for the number of recruits of a fish stock as a function of the number of
spawners. Its mechanism is a production per individual that declines exponentially with
density, $ae^{-bx}$, so that the total production of $x$ individuals is $axe^{-bx}$. In
fisheries the decline is attributed to competition among the young fish, for example
through cannibalism (Quinn and Deriso 1999), and the same form describes populations in
which fecundity falls with density (Hassell 1975; Royama 1992; Brännström and Sumpter
2005). The function is also used phenomenologically for any response that starts at zero,
peaks and falls. It is one of the two functions of
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd), where its properties are derived.

The function is

$$
f(x)=axe^{-bx},
$$

where $a$ is the initial slope and $b$ is the rate at which the production per individual
declines. Chapter 5 shows that

$$
f'(x)=a(1-bx)\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab(2-bx)\,e^{-bx},
$$

which gives a maximum at $x_{\max}=1/b$, with value $a/(be)$, and an
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) at $x=2/b$, where the
value is $2a/(be^2)$ and the decline is steepest. At the maximum the production per
individual is $ae^{-1}$, that is, 37% of what it is at low density.

In population ecology the function is written with a growth rate $r$ and a carrying
capacity $K$,

$$
f(x)=x\,e^{r(1-x/K)},
$$

which is the form above with $a=e^{r}$ and $b=r/K$. In this form $f(K)=K$: at the carrying
capacity the output equals the input. With the location of the peak as a parameter the
function is $axe^{-x/c}$, and the
[generalised Ricker](#sec-fn-generalised-ricker) function takes both the location and the
height of the peak as parameters.

## Logistic {#sec-fn-logistic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, symmetric around its midpoint} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{steepness (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{midpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/(1 + e^{bc}) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/2 \text{ and slope } ab/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \text{ with } a = 1,\ b = \beta_1,\ c = -\beta_0/\beta_1;\quad
\dfrac{K}{1 + \frac{K - n_0}{n_0}e^{-rx}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The logistic function describes a response that increases from a lower to an upper limit,
slowly at first, fastest half-way and slowly again. In population ecology it is the size
of a population whose growth rate per individual declines linearly with its density,
which is its mechanism (see Adler 2004). With an upper asymptote of 1 it
is the usual function for a probability that changes with a predictor, and in that role it
is phenomenological: it is chosen because it stays between 0 and 1. Verhulst (1838)
proposed the curve as a model for the growth of a population and later gave it its name
(*courbe logistique*).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{1+e^{-b(x-c)}},
$$

where $a$ is the upper asymptote, $b$ is the steepness and $c$ is the midpoint. The
function is defined for negative values of $x$ as well, so it has two ends. As
$x\to\infty$, $e^{-b(x-c)}\to0$ and $f(x)\to a$. As $x\to-\infty$ the exponential grows
without bound and $f(x)\to0$. So the function has two asymptotes, 0 and $a$. At $x=0$ its
value is $a/(1+e^{bc})$, which is small when $bc$ is large but is never zero.

For the derivative we write $f(x)=a\,u^{-1}$ with $u=1+e^{-b(x-c)}$ and apply the chain
rule:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}}{\left(1+e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^2}=b\,f(x)\left(1-\frac{f(x)}{a}\right),
$$

where the last equality follows from $f(x)/a=1/u$ and $1-f(x)/a=e^{-b(x-c)}/u$. It writes
the slope in terms of the function itself, which is convenient: the slope is close to zero
where $f(x)$ is close to 0 or to $a$, and it is largest in between. If we differentiate
$f'(x)=bf(x)-(b/a)f(x)^2$ once more with the chain rule, we obtain

$$
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)-\frac{2b}{a}\,f(x)\,f'(x)=b\,f'(x)\left(1-\frac{2f(x)}{a}\right).
$$

Since $f'(x)$ is positive everywhere, the second derivative is zero only where
$f(x)=a/2$, which happens at $x=c$ (there the exponential equals $e^{0}=1$). The function
is convex before that point and concave after it. So the midpoint $c$ is the
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) of the function: the
value of $x$ at which the function reaches half of its asymptote and at which it is
steepest. The slope at the midpoint is $f'(c)=b\,(a/2)(1-1/2)=ab/4$, so for a given
asymptote the parameter $b$ sets the maximum slope. The function is symmetric around its
midpoint: $f(c+s)+f(c-s)=a$ for any distance $s$.

To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve $f(x_p)=pa$,
which gives $e^{-b(x_p-c)}=(1-p)/p$ and

$$
x_p=c+\frac{1}{b}\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=c+\frac{\operatorname{logit}p}{b}.
$$

So the function reaches 90% of its asymptote at $c+\log(9)/b\approx c+2.2/b$ and 10% at
$c-2.2/b$. The distance between these two points, $4.4/b$, is a convenient way of reading
$b$ from a plot.

The logistic function has three forms that are in common use (see
[Reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)). The one of this
entry has the upper asymptote, the steepness and the midpoint as parameters. Statistical
texts write the function with an asymptote of 1 as the inverse logit of a straight line,

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_1x)}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}{1+e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}},
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $\beta_1$ the slope of the line. Comparing the
exponents, $\beta_1=b$ and $\beta_0=-bc$, so the midpoint is $c=-\beta_0/\beta_1$. In R
this form is `plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x)`. In population ecology, with time as the input,
the function is written as

$$
f(x)=\frac{K}{1+\dfrac{K-n_0}{n_0}\,e^{-rx}},
$$

where $K$ is the carrying capacity, $n_0$ is the size of the population at $x=0$ and $r$
is its growth rate per individual at low density. In this form the function is the
solution of a differential equation for the growth of a population, $dn/dt=rn(1-n/K)$,
which is where the parameters $r$ and $K$ come from (this book does not work with
dynamical models, so we use the function only as a curve). It is the form of this entry
with $a=K$, $b=r$ and $c=\log\left((K-n_0)/n_0\right)/r$. Some texts write the function
with the hyperbolic tangent, $\tfrac{a}{2}\left[1+\tanh\left(b(x-c)/2\right)\right]$,
which is again the same curve. A lower asymptote other than zero is obtained by adding a
parameter, $d+a/(1+e^{-b(x-c)})$, as in the [threshold](#sec-fn-threshold) entry.

## Gompertz {#sec-fn-gompertz}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, asymmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\exp\left(-e^{bc}\right) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/e \text{ and slope } ab/e \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right) \text{ with } d = e^{bc}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Gompertz function^[The function is named after Gompertz, who proposed in 1825 a law of
human mortality in which the death rate increases exponentially with age over much of
adult life; see Gompertz (1825).] is a sigmoid function like the logistic, with the
difference that it is asymmetric: it leaves its lower limit quickly and approaches its
upper limit slowly. It is used as an alternative to the logistic function for the growth
of organisms and of populations. It can be derived from the assumption that the relative
growth rate, $f'(x)/f(x)$, declines exponentially with $x$, as we show below. The practical
of [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) compares it with the logistic
function.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the upper asymptote, $b$ is a rate and $c$ is the location of the inflection
point. To analyse it we write $u=e^{-b(x-c)}$, so that $f(x)=ae^{-u}$. As $x\to\infty$,
$u\to0$ and $f(x)\to a$; as $x\to-\infty$, $u$ grows without bound and $f(x)\to0$. The
chain rule, with $du/dx=-bu$, gives

$$
f'(x)=ae^{-u}\times bu=b\,u\,f(x)=b\,f(x)\,\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right),
$$

where the last step uses $u=-\log\left(f(x)/a\right)$. The relative growth rate is
therefore $f'(x)/f(x)=bu=b\,e^{-b(x-c)}$, an exponential decay. Differentiating once more
with the product rule:

$$
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-b\,f'(x)
=b\,f'(x)\left[\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-1\right].
$$

Since $f'(x)$ is positive, the second derivative is zero only where $\log(a/f(x))=1$,
that is, where $f(x)=a/e$. This happens when $u=1$, at $x=c$. So the inflection point is
at $x=c$, where the function has reached $1/e\approx37\%$ of its asymptote (against 50%
for the logistic function) and its slope is $ab/e$. Half of the asymptote is reached later,
where $u=\log 2$, at $x=c-\log(\log 2)/b\approx c+0.37/b$.

The function is also written as $a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right)$, with $d=e^{bc}$. In that
form the value at zero is $ae^{-d}$ and the inflection point is at $x=\log d/b$.

## Bell-shaped {#sec-fn-gaussian}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2))| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, symmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{width (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty \text{ and as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = c \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = c \pm b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2} \text{ with } \beta_2 < 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The bell-shaped function, or Gaussian curve, describes a response that is highest at one
value of the predictor and declines symmetrically on both sides of it. In community
ecology it is the Gaussian response curve for the abundance of a species along an
environmental gradient (Gauch and Whittaker 1972), in which the location of the peak is
called the optimum of the species and the width its tolerance (ter Braak and Prentice
1988). It is also one of the functions used for the performance of an organism as a
function of its temperature (Angilletta 2006). It is a phenomenological function. Its formula is that of the probability density of the
[Normal distribution](distributions.qmd#sec-normal), multiplied by a constant so that the
height of the peak is a parameter; here it describes a curve and the area under it has no
role.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\,e^{-(x-c)^2/(2b^2)},
$$

where $a$ is the height of the peak, $c$ its location and $b$ its width. The parameter $c$
can take any value. The exponent is zero at $x=c$, where $f(c)=a$, and it becomes more and
more negative on both sides, so $f(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$. The chain
rule gives

$$
f'(x)=-\frac{x-c}{b^2}\,f(x),
\qquad
f''(x)=\left[\frac{(x-c)^2}{b^2}-1\right]\frac{f(x)}{b^2}.
$$

The slope is positive for $x<c$, zero at $x=c$ and negative for $x>c$, so the maximum is
at $c$. The second derivative is zero where $(x-c)^2=b^2$: the inflection points are at
$x=c\pm b$, where the function equals $a\,e^{-1/2}\approx0.61a$. The function is concave
between them and convex outside. If we solve $f(x)=a/2$ we find that the function is at
half of its height at $x=c\pm b\sqrt{2\log 2}\approx c\pm1.18b$.

The logarithm of the function is a parabola, so the function is the exponential of a
quadratic function, $e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2}$ with $\beta_2<0$ (a
[composition](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition)). Comparing the two forms
gives

$$
c=-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}, \qquad b=\sqrt{-\frac{1}{2\beta_2}}, \qquad
a=e^{\beta_0-\beta_1^2/(4\beta_2)}.
$$

For a probability, which cannot exceed 1, the corresponding function is the inverse logit
of a quadratic function, $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left[d-b(x-c)^2\right]$, which is
presented in Chapter 5 and used in the practical of
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd).

# Functions with a power parameter

In the functions of this group a parameter appears as an exponent. An exponent has no
units and changes the shape of a function, which makes these functions flexible. Most of
them contain one of the functions of the previous groups as a special case (see
[Nested functions](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions)).

## Power law {#sec-fn-power}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^b| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{monotonic: increasing when } b > 0,\ \text{decreasing when } b < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x > 0 \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ when } b > 0) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 1 \text{ (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x^b\text{)};\quad
b = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b > 0;\ \text{grows without bound when } b < 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } b > 0;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{none: multiplying } x \text{ by a factor } m \text{ multiplies } y \text{ by } m^b \text{ everywhere} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \log y = \log a + b\log x;\quad y_0\,(x/x_0)^b \text{ with } y_0 = a\,x_0^b
\end{aligned}
$$

The power law describes a response that changes by a constant proportion when the
predictor changes by a constant proportion. It is the function of allometry, the study of
how the properties of organisms change with their size: the reproductive biomass of plants
as a function of the diameter of their stem (Niklas 1993) and the metabolic rate of
animals as a function of their body mass (Etienne et al. 2006) are two examples. It is
also used for the number of species as a function of the area sampled (Tjørve 2003) and
for the fractal properties of landscapes (Halley et al. 2004). A power law is mechanistic
when it follows from geometry (the surface of an organism is proportional to the square of
its length and its volume to the cube), and many other mechanisms lead to power laws
(Mitzenmacher 2003), so the function alone says little about the process behind it.

The function is

$$
f(x)=ax^{b},
$$

where $b$ is the exponent, which can be positive or negative, and $a$ is the value of the
function at $x=1$. The two ends depend on the sign of $b$. When $b>0$ the function starts
at zero and grows without bound; when $b<0$ it is unbounded as $x\to0$ and tends to zero
as $x\to\infty$. The power rule gives

$$
f'(x)=ab\,x^{b-1}=b\,\frac{f(x)}{x}, \qquad f''(x)=ab(b-1)\,x^{b-2}.
$$

The function is convex when $b>1$ or $b<0$, concave when $0<b<1$ and a straight line
through the origin when $b=1$. Rearranging the first derivative gives

$$
\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{b}{x},
$$

which says that a small relative change in $x$ produces a relative change in $y$ that is
$b$ times as large: an increase of 1% in $x$ changes $y$ by about $b$%. For a change of any
size, $f(mx)=a(mx)^{b}=m^{b}f(x)$, so multiplying $x$ by $m$ multiplies $y$ by $m^{b}$,
whatever the value of $x$. It follows that the power law has no characteristic scale and no
half-maximum. It has no upper asymptote either; when $b<0$ it has a horizontal asymptote at
zero, which it approaches as $x\to\infty$. This is the main difference from the exponential function,
in which it is a fixed step added to $x$ that multiplies $y$ by a constant factor.

Taking logarithms gives $\log f(x)=\log a+b\log x$: on a plot with two logarithmic axes
the power law is a straight line with slope $b$. The
units of $a$ are awkward, since they depend on $b$. They become those of $y$ if we write
the function with a reference value $x_0$ of the predictor,

$$
f(x)=y_0\left(\frac{x}{x_0}\right)^{b}, \qquad y_0=a\,x_0^{b},
$$

where $y_0$ is the value of the function at $x=x_0$.

## von Bertalanffy {#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating (simple form)};\quad \text{sigmoid (generalised form)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq c \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptotic size (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{growth rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the size is zero (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right),\ \text{slope } ab\,e^{bc} \quad (c \leq 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the asymptote at } x = c + \log 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a - (a - y_0)\,e^{-bx} \text{ with } y_0 = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right);\quad
a\left(1 - e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)} \text{ (generalised form)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The von Bertalanffy function describes the size of an organism as a function of its age.
It is the usual growth curve in fisheries and it is a mechanistic function (von
Bertalanffy 1938): it follows from a balance between the energy that an organism
assimilates and the energy that it spends on maintenance (Essington et al. 2001). In its
simple form, which is used for body length, it is a
[saturating exponential](#sec-fn-monomolecular) function that is shifted along $x$. In its
generalised form, which is used for body mass, the saturating exponential is raised to a
power, and the function becomes sigmoid.

The simple form is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the asymptotic size, $b$ is the growth rate and $c$ is the age at which the
function is zero. An organism has a positive size at birth, so $c$ is zero or negative
when $x$ is the age since birth: it is where the curve would start if we extended it
backwards, and it is a
[location parameter](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts) with no biological
meaning of its own. The properties are those of the saturating exponential function, moved
by $c$. The size at birth is $f(0)=a\left(1-e^{bc}\right)$, the function tends to $a$ as
$x\to\infty$, and its derivative,

$$
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}=b\left(a-f(x)\right),
$$

is positive and decreases with age, so growth is fastest at birth and the function is
concave. Half of the asymptotic size is reached at $x=c+\log 2/b$. Since the size at birth
is easier to interpret than $c$, the function is also written as
$a-(a-y_0)\,e^{-bx}$ with $y_0=f(0)$.

The generalised form is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)},
$$

where $d$ is an exponent between 0 and 1, without units. It is the size of an organism
that gains mass at a rate proportional to its mass raised to the power $d$ and loses mass
at a rate proportional to its mass; the rate $b$ is then $1-d$ times the rate of loss.
With $d=0$ the exponent $1/(1-d)$ is 1 and we recover the simple form, so the simple form
is [nested](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions) in the generalised one. The
value $d=2/3$ is often used, on the argument that assimilation is proportional to a
surface (a length squared) and mass to a volume (a length cubed) (Quinn and Deriso 1999).
The exponent is then 3, and the function is the cube of the simple form: if length follows
the simple form and mass is proportional to the cube of length, mass follows the
generalised form with $d=2/3$ and the same $b$ and $c$.

To find the landmarks of the generalised form we write $m=1/(1-d)$ and
$u=e^{-b(x-c)}$, so that $f(x)=a(1-u)^m$ and $du/dx=-bu$. The chain rule and then the
product rule give

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= abm\,u\,(1-u)^{m-1}, \\
f''(x) &= -ab^2m\,u\,(1-u)^{m-2}\left(1-mu\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

For $m>1$ the slope is zero at $x=c$, where $u=1$, and the second derivative changes sign
where $u=1/m$. So the generalised form has an inflection point at

$$
x=c+\frac{\log m}{b}, \qquad \text{with value } a\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}=a\,d^{\,1/(1-d)}.
$$

For $d=2/3$ the inflection point is at $c+\log 3/b$, where the function equals
$(2/3)^3a=8a/27\approx0.30\,a$: an organism that follows this function gains mass fastest
when it has reached 30% of its final mass.

## Shepherd {#sec-fn-shepherd}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x^c)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x^c\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = \left(b/(c-1)\right)^{1/c} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{1 + (x/k)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b \text{ and } k = b^{1/c}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Shepherd function is a [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function in which
the $x$ of the denominator is raised to a power. It is used for the output of a population
(recruits, seeds, the adults of the next generation) as a function of its density, when
the strength of the competition among individuals is to be estimated from the data
(Maynard Smith and Slatkin 1973; Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The exponent $c$ sets that
strength. With $c=1$ the function is the Michaelis–Menten function and the output levels
off. With $c<1$ the output keeps increasing with density, and with $c>1$ it declines at
high density, as it does for the [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) function; population ecologists
call the two cases undercompensating and overcompensating density dependence. In
fisheries Shepherd (1982) proposed the function for the number of recruits, as a
generalisation of the Beverton–Holt curve, and it can be derived from a mortality of the
young fish that depends on the initial size of their cohort (Quinn and Deriso 1999).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x^{c}},
$$

where $c$ is the exponent and $a$ and $b$ are positive. The units of $a$ and $b$ depend on
$c$, which makes them hard to interpret, so we first look for landmarks. For small $x$
the term $x^c$ is negligible next to $b$ and $f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x$: the initial slope is
$a/b$. For large $x$ the term $b$ is negligible next to $x^c$ and $f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}$,
which grows without bound when $c<1$, equals $a$ when $c=1$ and tends to zero when $c>1$.
The quotient rule gives

$$
f'(x)=\frac{a\left(b+x^{c}\right)-ax\times cx^{c-1}}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x^{c}\right]}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}.
$$

When $c\le1$ the numerator is positive for every $x$ and the function increases
throughout. When $c>1$ the numerator is zero where $x^c=b/(c-1)$, so the function has a
maximum at

$$
x_{\max}=\left(\frac{b}{c-1}\right)^{1/c},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)}{bc}\,x_{\max},
$$

where the value follows from replacing $x^c$ by $b/(c-1)$ in the denominator.

The function is easier to read with the initial slope $s=a/b$ and the scale $k=b^{1/c}$
as parameters, which we obtain by dividing the numerator and the denominator by $b$:

$$
f(x)=\frac{sx}{1+(x/k)^{c}}.
$$

In this [reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation) $k$ has the
units of $x$ and $s$ those of $y$ per unit of $x$. At $x=k$ the denominator equals 2
whatever the value of $c$, so $k$ is the density at which the output is half of what the
initial slope alone would give, $sk/2$. The exponent then decides what happens beyond
$k$, and the maximum for $c>1$ is at $k\,(c-1)^{-1/c}$.

## Hassell {#sec-fn-hassell}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x)^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b^c \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = b/(c-1) \text{ and inflection point at } x = 2b/(c-1) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{(1 + x/b)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b^c \text{ the initial slope}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Hassell function is a [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function in which
the whole denominator is raised to a power. Hassell (1975) proposed it for the density
dependence of populations with discrete generations, such as those of many insects, and it
is used in the same way as the [Shepherd](#sec-fn-shepherd) function, from which it
differs in where the exponent is placed. The exponent $c$ again sets the strength of the
competition: the output keeps increasing with density when $c<1$, levels off when $c=1$
and declines at high density when $c>1$. The function is often used phenomenologically, to
let the data decide among these three cases. A mechanistic derivation also exists.
Brännström and Sumpter (2005) considered individuals that compete for the resources of
separate sites: when the individuals are distributed at random among the sites the result
is the [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) function, and when they are clustered, following a
[Negative Binomial distribution](distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial), it is the
Hassell function.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{(b+x)^{c}},
$$

where $c$ is the exponent, $b$ has the units of $x$ and $a$ has units that depend on $c$.
For small $x$ the denominator is close to $b^c$, so the initial slope is $a/b^c$. For
large $x$ the denominator is close to $x^c$ and $f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}$, which gives the
same three cases as for the Shepherd function. The quotient rule, with the chain rule for
the denominator, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{a\,(b+x)^{c}-ax\times c\,(b+x)^{c-1}}{(b+x)^{2c}}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x\right]}{(b+x)^{c+1}}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{ac\left[(c-1)\,x-2b\right]}{(b+x)^{c+2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

When $c\le1$ the slope is positive for every $x$. When $c>1$ the numerator of the first
derivative is zero at

$$
x_{\max}=\frac{b}{c-1},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)^{c-1}}{c^{\,c}\,b^{\,c-1}},
$$

which is a maximum, and the numerator of the second derivative is zero at $x=2b/(c-1)$,
an inflection point on the way down. As for the Ricker function, the inflection point is
at twice the location of the maximum. The value of the maximum follows from
$b+x_{\max}=bc/(c-1)$; for $c=2$ it is $a/(4b)$ and for $c=3$ it is $4a/(27b^2)$.

The resemblance to the Ricker function has a reason. With the initial slope as a
parameter the function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{sx}{(1+x/b)^{c}}, \qquad s=\frac{a}{b^{c}},
$$

and if we let $c$ grow while we keep the ratio $c/b$ at a fixed value $\beta$, the term
$(1+\beta x/c)^{-c}$ tends to $e^{-\beta x}$. So the Hassell function has the
Michaelis–Menten function at one end of its range ($c=1$) and approaches the Ricker
function $sxe^{-\beta x}$ at the other.

## Generalised Ricker {#sec-fn-generalised-ricker}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, of adjustable width} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0;\ \text{slope } 0 \text{ when } c > 1,\ ae/b \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = b \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = b\left(1 \pm 1/\sqrt{c}\right) \text{ (only the upper one when } c \leq 1\text{)} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b} \text{ with } a' = a\,(e/b)^{c};\quad
\text{with } c = 1,\ \text{the Ricker function } (ae/b)\,x\,e^{-x/b}
\end{aligned}
$$

The generalised Ricker function describes a response with a single peak whose location,
height and width are three separate parameters. In the [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) function
one parameter controls both where the peak is and how fast the function declines beyond
it, so a peak that is far from zero is necessarily wide; the exponent of the generalised
function removes that link. Persson et al. (1998) used it for the attack rate of a
predator as a function of its body mass, and in fisheries it has been proposed for the
number of recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Quinn and Deriso
1999). It is a phenomenological function. [Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions)
uses it for the number of tadpoles killed as a function of their body length. Bellows
(1981) proposed another generalisation of the Ricker function, in which the power is
placed inside the exponential.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\left[\frac{x}{b}\,e^{1-x/b}\right]^{c},
$$

where $a$ is the height of the peak, $b$ is its location and $c$ is a positive exponent.
The term in brackets is a Ricker function that is written so that its maximum is at
$x=b$ and has a value of 1. The function is zero at $x=0$, and it tends to zero as
$x\to\infty$ because the exponential dominates the power of $x$. The derivative is easiest
to find from the logarithm of the function,
$\log f(x)=\log a+c\left[\log(x/b)+1-x/b\right]$, whose derivative is $f'(x)/f(x)$:

$$
f'(x)=c\,f(x)\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right).
$$

The slope is positive for $x<b$, zero at $x=b$ and negative for $x>b$, whatever the value
of $c$: the maximum is at $x=b$, where the term in brackets equals 1 and $f(b)=a$.
Differentiating once more with the product rule gives

$$
f''(x)=c\,f(x)\left[c\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right],
$$

which is zero where $\sqrt{c}\,\left|1-x/b\right|=1$. So the inflection points are at

$$
x=b\left(1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\right),
$$

one on each side of the peak when $c>1$. The distance between them, $2b/\sqrt{c}$, is a
measure of the width of the peak: a peak that is half as wide needs an exponent that is
four times as large. When $c\le1$ the lower value is zero or negative and is not an
inflection point (with $c=1$ it is $x=0$, where the second derivative is $-2ae/b^2$ and
not zero), so the only inflection point is the upper one. With $c=1$ it is at $2b$, as for
the Ricker function. Near its peak the function is close to the
[bell-shaped](#sec-fn-gaussian) function with height $a$, location $b$ and width
$b/\sqrt{c}$.

With $c=1$ the function is $(ae/b)\,xe^{-x/b}$, a Ricker function with an initial slope
$ae/b$ and a rate $1/b$. For any $c$ the function can be multiplied out to
$a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b}$ with $a'=a\,(e/b)^{c}$, a power of $x$ multiplied by an exponential,
which is the form in which it is often printed.

## Non-rectangular hyperbola {#sec-fn-nonrectangular}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|(s + p_max - sqrt((s + p_max)^2 - 4 * theta * s * p_max)) / (2 * theta)|,\ \text{with } \texttt{s = alpha * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a bend of adjustable sharpness} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < p_{\max} \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad \alpha = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
p_{\max} = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad \theta = \text{sharpness of the bend (no units)},\ 0 < \theta \leq 1 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } \alpha \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to p_{\max},\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{at } x = p_{\max}/\alpha \text{ the function equals } p_{\max}/\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - \theta}\right) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the smaller root } y \text{ of } \theta y^2 - (\alpha x + p_{\max})\,y + \alpha x\,p_{\max} = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The non-rectangular hyperbola describes the rate of photosynthesis of a leaf as a function
of the light that it receives. It is a saturating function with three parameters: the
initial slope, the asymptote and the sharpness of the bend between the two. It is derived
from principles of plant physiology (Thornley 2002), so it is a mechanistic function, and
its parameters have their own symbols in that field: $\alpha$ is the efficiency with which
the leaf uses light when light is scarce, $p_{\max}$ is the rate of photosynthesis when
light is abundant and $\theta$ is the sharpness. We keep these symbols here. In the terms
of the [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function, $p_{\max}$ is the asymptote
$a$ and $\alpha$ is the initial slope $a/b$.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{\alpha x+p_{\max}-\sqrt{\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)^2-4\,\theta\,\alpha x\,p_{\max}}}{2\,\theta},
$$

where $x$ is the light received by the leaf. The formula is the smaller of the two
solutions of a quadratic equation in $y=f(x)$,

$$
\theta\,y^2-\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y+\alpha x\,p_{\max}=0,
$$

and the properties of the function are easier to derive from this equation than from the
formula. If we move the term $(1-\theta)\,y^2$ to the right-hand side, the left-hand side
can be factorised:

$$
\left(\alpha x-y\right)\left(p_{\max}-y\right)=(1-\theta)\,y^2 .
$$

The two factors on the left are the distances from $y$ to the straight line $\alpha x$ and
to the plateau $p_{\max}$. This form shows the two extremes of the function. When
$\theta=1$ the right-hand side is zero, so one of the two factors has to be zero: $y$ is
either on the line or on the plateau, and the smaller root is $\min(\alpha x,p_{\max})$, a
[hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) function with a breakpoint at $x=p_{\max}/\alpha$.
When $\theta=0$ the quadratic term of the equation vanishes and what remains is
$\alpha x\,p_{\max}=\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y$, that is,

$$
y=\frac{\alpha x\,p_{\max}}{\alpha x+p_{\max}}=\frac{p_{\max}\,x}{p_{\max}/\alpha+x},
$$

a Michaelis–Menten function with an asymptote $p_{\max}$ and a half-maximum
$p_{\max}/\alpha$. (The formula itself cannot be evaluated at $\theta=0$, as it divides by
zero; the Michaelis–Menten function is its limit as $\theta\to0$.) Both functions are
therefore [nested](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions) in the non-rectangular
hyperbola, and values of $\theta$ between 0 and 1 give curves between them.

The limits follow from the same form. At $x=0$ the equation is satisfied by $y=0$. For
small $x$ and $y$, the term $y^2$ is negligible and $p_{\max}-y\approx p_{\max}$, so
$y\approx\alpha x$: the initial slope is $\alpha$ for every $\theta$. Dividing both sides
by $\alpha x$ gives $(1-y/(\alpha x))(p_{\max}-y)=(1-\theta)\,y^2/(\alpha x)$, whose
right-hand side tends to zero as $x\to\infty$ since $y$ stays below $p_{\max}$, so
$f(x)\to p_{\max}$.

The parameter $\theta$ can be read at one particular value of $x$. At $x=p_{\max}/\alpha$,
where the line $\alpha x$ crosses the plateau, the equation becomes
$\theta y^2-2p_{\max}\,y+p_{\max}^2=0$, and its smaller root is

$$
f\left(\frac{p_{\max}}{\alpha}\right)=\frac{p_{\max}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)}{\theta}
=\frac{p_{\max}}{1+\sqrt{1-\theta}} .
$$

At this value of $x$ the function is at half of its asymptote when $\theta=0$, at two
thirds when $\theta=0.75$ and on the asymptote when $\theta=1$. The sharpness is hard to
estimate from data (Thornley 2002), because it only affects the function around the bend.

Leaves also respire, so that their net exchange of carbon dioxide is negative in the dark.
This is described by subtracting the rate of respiration from the function, which is a
[shift along $y$](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts).

## Richards {#sec-fn-richards}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, of adjustable asymmetry} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \text{ when } d > 0;\quad x \geq c + \log(-d)/b \text{ when } -1 \leq d < 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)};\quad d = \text{shape (no units)},\ d \geq -1,\ d \neq 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/\left(1 + d\,e^{bc}\right)^{1/d} \\
